title: Come to Our Pumpkin Party
text:
Dear Neighbors,
You are invited to our Halloween pumpkin party! It will be on Saturday afternoon in our garage, which Dad has decorated with orange lights and {plural noun}.

Please come wearing your most {adjective} costume. Last year Uncle Sal came dressed as a {noun}, and nobody knew who he was until he started {verb ending in ing}. There will be a prize for the best costume and a smaller prize for the most {adjective} one.

We will paint pumpkins, play pumpkin bowling, and bob for {plural noun}. Grandpa will play {adjective} music on his old radio. Mom is making cupcakes with {color} frosting and little {plural noun} on top. Our dog, Noodle, will be dressed as a {animal}, so please pet him {adverb}.

At six o'clock, everyone will go trick-or-treating together. Please bring a bag, a flashlight, and {number} friends. We can't wait to {verb} with you!
Love,
The Garcia Family

title: How to Decorate a Pumpkin
text:
Decorating a pumpkin is one of the best parts of fall. All you need is paint, glue, and a {adjective} grown-up.

First, pick the right pumpkin. Find one that is round, orange, and about the size of a {noun}. Wash it {adverb} and dry it with a towel.

Next, paint a face. Give it two {adjective} eyes, a triangle nose, and a big smile full of {plural noun}. For eyebrows, use two {plural noun}. For a hat, glue a {food} on top.

Last, put your pumpkin on the front porch next to the {noun}. When kids walk by, they will {verb} and point. My pumpkin last year looked so {adjective} that my neighbor {past tense verb} every time he walked past. This year, I am naming my pumpkin {name}. I hope it does not start {verb ending in ing} again.

title: The Costume Parade Winners
text:
Thank you to everyone who marched in the Oak Street School Costume Parade! The judges had a very {adjective} job. Here are this year's winners.

The prize for Funniest Costume goes to Eli, who came dressed as a giant {noun}. He waddled down the hall {adverb} and waved at every class. He wins a pumpkin pencil and a bag of {plural noun}.

The prize for Most Creative goes to the Lee twins. They dressed up together as one {adjective} {animal} with four legs and two heads. The costume took {number} hours to make and smells a little bit like {plural noun}.

The prize for Best Teacher Costume goes to Mrs. Hart. She wore a cape made of {plural noun} and a hat shaped like a {noun}. When she won, she {past tense verb} right there in the gym. Next year, the judges hope everyone will {verb} in the parade. Have a {adjective} Halloween!

title: Friendly Ghost Cookies
text:
These cookies look like little ghosts, but they are very friendly and a little bit {adjective}. Ask a grown-up to help with the oven and the {plural noun}.

First, mix one cup of sugar, two cups of flour, and a spoonful of {food} in a big bowl. Stir it {adverb} until there are no lumps. Roll the dough flat with a {noun} and cut out ghost shapes.

Bake the cookies for {number} minutes. While you wait, you can {verb} around the kitchen like a ghost. Say "boo" very quietly so the cookies do not get {adjective}.

When the cookies are cool, cover them with white frosting. Use two chocolate chips for eyes and a tiny {noun} for the mouth. Some people add {plural noun} on top, too. If you are very quiet, you might hear your ghosts {verb ending in ing}. My little sister says they taste like {plural noun} and {adjective} dreams.

title: My Trick-or-Treat Night
text:
Dear Diary,
Tonight was Halloween! I dressed up as a {adjective} {noun}. Mom took three days to make my costume, and it has {plural noun} glued all over it. It is hard to walk in, but I love it.

At six o'clock, Dad and I went trick-or-treating. Dad was dressed as a {adjective} pirate. The first house had a blow-up pumpkin wearing {plural noun}. The lady at the door said my costume was very {adjective}. She gave me two candies and a {noun}.

At the next house, a man was dressed as a friendly ghost. He {past tense verb} when he saw me, and then we both laughed. Then I saw my friend Zoe. She was dressed as a {animal} and was {verb ending in ing} down the sidewalk.

At home, I counted {number} pieces of candy. Mom let me pick two to eat {adverb}. Now I am in bed, still wearing my costume. Tomorrow I am going to wear it to breakfast and {verb} until Mom says stop.

title: Rules for Trick-or-Treating
text:
Trick-or-treating is fun, but there are rules. My big sister Mae wrote these for me, and she says they are very {adjective}.

Rule one: Always walk with a grown-up and carry a {adjective} flashlight. Rule two: Only go to houses with the porch light on. If a pumpkin looks like a {noun}, they have the good candy.

Rule three: Say "Trick or treat!" in a {adjective} voice. Then say thank you {adverb} and wave your {body part}. Never take more than {number} pieces. Rule four: If a house gives out {plural noun} instead of candy, say thank you anyway.

Rule five: Do not eat anything until Mom checks it. You may {verb} while you wait. Then you can trade. Mae will trade one chocolate bar for three {plural noun}. Rule six: Hide your bag somewhere {adjective}. Last year, Dad found my bag while he was {verb ending in ing} in the closet. Next year, I am going to hide it inside a {noun}.

title: A Letter from Boo the Friendly Ghost
text:
Dear Kids of Pine Street,
My name is Boo, and I am the friendly ghost who lives in the attic of the yellow house. I am very {adjective}, and I love to play. During the day, I sleep in an old box of {plural noun} under a {adjective} blanket.

Every Halloween, I float around and look at the costumes. Last year, I saw a boy dressed as a {noun}, a girl dressed as a giant {food}, and a baby dressed as a {adjective} {noun}. I {past tense verb} so hard that I floated into a tree.

My favorite things are pumpkins, warm socks, and {plural noun}. Candy falls through me, but I like to smell it. I also like to {verb} when the moon is out and sing {adverb} to the owls.

This year, I will sit on my porch. If you see me, please wave and say "{silly word}." That means hello in ghost. I will wave back with my {adjective} little hands.
Your friend,
Boo

title: Big News on Maple Lane
text:
Good evening. This is Kip Moore with Halloween news from Maple Lane, where every house is decorated for the big night.

At the blue house, the Wilsons put up a giant blow-up {animal} that is taller than their roof. It has {number} glowing eyes and a hat made of {plural noun}. Neighbors say it is very {adjective}.

Next door, Mr. Patel covered his porch in orange lights and {plural noun}. When kids ring his doorbell, a {adjective} song plays and a toy pumpkin starts {verb ending in ing}. Kids have been lining up to {verb} on his steps all day.

At the corner house, Mrs. Ruiz painted her pumpkins to look like {plural noun}. She waved {adverb} at our camera and gave us each a {noun}. Tonight, the whole street will turn on its lights at seven o'clock. Experts say it will be {adjective}. Back to you, {name}!

title: The Official Candy Trading Guide
text:
After trick-or-treating, my friends and I trade candy. Here is our official trading guide.

One lollipop is worth two little chocolate bars. One big chocolate bar is worth {number} lollipops. A box of raisins is worth one sticker and a {noun}. Raisins are my cousin Ava's favorite, so this is a {adjective} deal.

If you get something odd, like a toothbrush or a bag of {plural noun}, trade it to my dad. He will give you one penny and a {adjective} high five. He says he is {verb ending in ing} for a good cause.

When trading, sit up straight and talk {adverb}. No grabbing, and no {verb ending in ing}. If two people want the same candy, they have to {verb} for it. Last year, Ava {past tense verb} for an hour to win a gummy worm. The winner gets the candy, and the other person gets a {adjective} hug. At the end, everyone puts their candy in a {color} bowl, and Mom says it is time to brush our {plural noun}.

title: Welcome to the Not-Scary House
text:
Welcome to the Not-Scary House! My name is Ruby, and I will be your tour guide. Please stay with the group and keep your hands inside your {plural noun}.

Our first stop is the front hall. Here you will see a friendly ghost made from an old bedsheet and two {plural noun}. His name is Gus, and he loves to {verb}. If you shake his hand, he might say something {adjective}.

Next is the kitchen, where the cat is wearing a {adjective} hat. The bowl on the table is full of green slime made of {food} and jelly. Please do not touch it. My brother touched it last year, and his {body part} was sticky for {number} days.

Our last stop is the living room, where the jack-o'-lanterns are {verb ending in ing} on the windowsill. Each one has a {adjective} face. Before you leave, take a {noun} from the basket by the door and say goodbye {adverb}. Come back next year, when we will have even more {plural noun}!
